claims.text: Edward Jones: The 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states Edward Jones is targeting new clients through a new digital platform focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors, indicating the firm's view, in its own words, that the digital channel is central to serving younger, next-generation investors; the firm describes this as one initiative among those targeting new clients, including High Net Worth and Workplace initiatives.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 3Q25 earnings call (September 2025), management said younger investors at Schwab are highly engaged in building wealth over the long term, with one-third of retail households that created a financial plan within the last two years being under age 40.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 2Q25 earnings call (June 2025), management said investors and traders of all ages, including younger investors, are turning to Schwab to invest in digital assets through ETFs, futures, and closed-end funds.
The Charles Schwab Corporation: The 2026 investor day deck reports that 42% of thinkorswim users are Millennial or Gen Z.

Industry research: The 2024 Bank of America Private Bank study states that among investors ages 21-43, the greatest opportunities for growth are real estate investments (31%), crypto/digital assets (28%), private equity (26%), personal company/brand (24%), direct investment into companies (22%), and companies focused on positive impact (21%).

Industry research: The 2026 Bank of America Private Bank study states that Gen Z and Millennial younger investors allocate 32 percent of their portfolio to stocks, compared with 58 percent for Gen X and Baby Boomer older investors.
Industry research: The 2026 Bank of America Private Bank study states that 42% of younger respondents own art; among those who do not, 75% are interested in owning art, and 94% own collectables.
Industry research: The 2026 Bank of America Private Bank study states that 47% of young investors use AI to research companies or markets.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 3Q25 earnings call (September 2025), management said younger investors' top online resource for investing information is YouTube, and that Schwab is the number one financial services firm on YouTube by followers.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 3Q25 earnings call (September 2025), management said younger traders are turning to Schwab because they recognize the potential trading has in helping build wealth over time, and because Schwab has the platforms, tools, education, coaching, expertise, and service they need to succeed.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: The 2026 investor day deck associates younger investors with self-directed offerings, listing Schwab Starter Kit, Schwab Teen Investor Account, and no/low commissions for that segment.
Industry research: The 2026 Bank of America Private Bank study states that 65% of young investors still prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor.
Industry research: The 2026 Bank of America Private Bank study states that 87% of young investors are comfortable with advisors using AI to help manage portfolios.

Industry research: Cerulli research (October 2025) states that while older investors tend to be more advisor-reliant, younger investors prefer to retain a greater degree of control of at least part of their investing lives.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 4Q24 earnings call (December 2024), management said Schwab reported 33% of its new-to-firm retail households were under age 30, and more than 50% under age 40 (full year 2024).

The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 2Q25 earnings call (June 2025), management said more than 30% of Schwab's new-to-firm clients in the first half of 2025 were under age 30, and nearly 60% under age 40.
The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 3Q26 earnings call (September 2026), management said approximately 70% of new-to-firm retail households are Gen Z and millennials.
The Charles Schwab Corporation: The 3Q26 deck (period ended September 30, 2026) reports approximately 70% of new-to-firm retail households are Gen Z and Millennials.
The Charles Schwab Corporation: The 2026 investor day deck reports that 61% of new clients are Gen Z and Millennial investors, and over 60% of new-to-firm retail households are under age 40.

Edward Jones: The 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) identifies evolving generational wealth transfer and changing client expectations for expanded product offerings and technology needs, and changing client demographics, preferences and values, as a risk to its ability to compete and adapt its business model.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: The 2026 investor day deck lists the Schwab Starter Kit, the Schwab Teen Investor Account, and no/low commissions among the offerings it deploys for younger investors.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 3Q25 earnings call (September 2025), management said Schwab puts on 35 hours a week of live content for investors about how to learn to trade and invest, including the power of compounding.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 3Q25 earnings call (September 2025), management said what Schwab offers the young investor is support, service, and education, plus the leading trading platform thinkorswim and its digital capabilities.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 2Q25 earnings call (June 2025), management cited in-person experiences in over 400 locations and 16,000 advisors in every community where young investors can walk in and talk about paying off college debt or buying a house.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 2Q26 earnings call (June 2026), management attributed growth in young investors partly to the removal of commissions, which brought more people with less money into the market.

Edward Jones: The 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) lists among its aspirations 'Attract and serve new client segments' and 'Anticipate clients' needs with the right offering at the right time, now and for generations to come.'

Edward Jones: The 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states Edward Jones seeks to address generational wealth transfer, changing client demographics, preferences and values through its initiatives to deliver enhanced value for current and potential clients.

Edward Jones: A trade publication (August 2026) observes that Edward Jones chose Quicken—a personal financial management software originating in the DOS era more than 40 years ago—rather than buying Mint.com from Intuit or investing in a more modern platform such as Monarch Money, which already has a For-Advisor-Professionals version.

Edward Jones: A trade publication (August 2026) reports the advisor industry has built personal financial management solutions beyond Edward Jones, including eMoney's personal financial management dashboard, Envestnet's acquisition of Yodlee alongside MoneyGuide, and RightCapital's financial dashboard and budgeting tools; direct-to-consumer tools include Mint.com and Monarch Money.

Edward Jones: A trade publication (August 2026) characterizes the Quicken deal as another negative harbinger for MoneyGuide, interpreting it as a vote of no confidence from Edward Jones that MoneyGuide can deliver a comprehensive financial planning value proposition.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 3Q26 earnings call (September 2026), management said Schwab is attracting younger clients, with approximately 70% of new-to-firm retail households being Gen Z and millennials (also reported in the 3Q26 deck).

The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 3Q25 earnings call (September 2025), management said nearly one-third of new-to-firm retail households at Schwab are Gen Zers, investors between the ages of 13 and 28.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 4Q25 earnings call (December 2025), management said Gen Z investors comprise nearly a third of new retail client accounts opened in 2025, and nearly 60% of new retail clients are under age 40.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 2Q25 earnings call (June 2025), management said one in six new-to-firm retail households are under age 24, more than 30% of new-to-firm clients are under age 30, and nearly 60% are under age 40.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 4Q24 earnings call (December 2024), management said Schwab is attracting younger investors, with 33% of new-to-firm retail households under age 30 and more than 50% under age 40.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 4Q25 earnings call (December 2025), management said the average age of Schwab's client has fallen by about 10 years in the last decade and is now in the 40s, and a third of its new-to-firm clients last year were Gen Z investors.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: The 2026 investor day deck lists Schwab Starter Kit, Schwab Teen Investor Account, and no/low commissions among its initiatives for younger investors, and reports 42% of thinkorswim users are Millennial or Gen Z, over 60% of new-to-firm retail households are under age 40, and 61% of new clients are Gen Z and Millennial investors.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 3Q25 earnings call (September 2025), management said Schwab provides 35 hours a week of live content to teach investors how to trade and invest, and one-third of retail households who created a financial plan within the last two years are under age 40.

Comparison: On this evidence, a direct like-for-like comparison of Edward Jones's disclosures and initiatives for younger investors against those of competitors is not valid. Edward Jones discloses qualitative initiatives (a digital platform for Next Generation investors, Financial Planning Services, a Quicken minority stake) but no younger-investor growth metrics, whereas Schwab discloses both specific initiatives (Schwab Starter Kit, Teen Investor Account, no/low commissions, 35 hours weekly of live content) and quantified younger-investor growth figures (e.g., ~70% of new-to-firm retail households being Gen Z and millennials, 61% of new clients Gen Z/Millennial). The two firms' young-investor growth figures rest on unverified metric definitions, so those figures cannot be compared across firms; and Morgan Stanley and Raymond James Financial produce no such disclosures in the documents searched, while Merrill's disclosures concern its own under-40 financial advisors rather than younger clients.

a1.all.label: fact

items.text: According to Cerulli, younger investors are typically more comfortable directing their own investing through online brokerages, so financial advisors seeking these clients must articulate benefits outside the investing realm, such as financial planning, lending, and tax services.
items.quote: Younger investors typically are more comfortable directing their own investing through online brokerages (e.g., E*TRADE, Fidelity), meaning financial advisors looking to connect with these prospective clients must be able to articulate benefits outside of the investing realm, such as financial planning, lending, and tax services.

items.text: Cerulli finds that while older investors tend to be more advisor-reliant, younger investors prefer to retain a greater degree of control of at least part of their investing lives.
items.quote: While older investors tend to be more advisor-reliant, younger investors prefer to retain a greater degree of control of at least part of their investing lives.

items.text: Schwab states that younger clients learn about finances primarily through social media and family, and that being met in those channels is a reason they turn to the firm.
items.quote: We know they learn about finances primarily through social media and family.

items.text: Schwab states that younger traders turn to it because they recognize trading's potential to build wealth over time and because of its platforms, tools, education, coaching, expertise, and service.
items.quote: Younger traders are turning to us because they recognize the potential that trading has in helping build wealth over time. And they are turning to Schwab because we have the platforms, tools, education, coaching, expertise, and service they need to help them succeed

items.text: Bank of America Private Bank's study finds that 65% of young investors still prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor.
items.quote: sixty five percent 65% still prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor.

items.text: Schwab's CEO stated that young new-to-firm clients (a third are Gen Zers under age 28) seek financial planning conversations, want to consolidate loans (e.g., into a Pledged Asset Line to pay off student debt), want advice on buying a house in the future, and want to be long-term investors who need help navigating.
items.quote: They're responsible for a lot of the financial planning conversations that we've had. They'll come in and want to consolidate loans into a Pledged Asset Line balance so they can pay off their student debt. They'll talk to us about how to buy a house in the future. These are clients that really want to be investors for the long term and want our help navigating it.

a1.all.reason: Cerulli research states how younger investors approach investing and what advisors must offer to attract them, which is directly about factors driving clients under 40.

a2.all.label: different_quantity

items.text: Schwab CEO Rick Wurster states that younger clients (Gen Z, ages 13-28) learn about finances primarily through social media and family, which is why Schwab meets them in those channels.
items.quote: We know they learn about finances primarily through social media and family.
items.scope: younger (Gen Z) retail clients at Schwab

items.text: Schwab CEO Rick Wurster states that younger investors' top online resource is YouTube, and Schwab is the number one financial services firm on YouTube by followers.
items.quote: Their top online resource is YouTube, and we're the number one financial services firm on YouTube by followers.

items.text: The CFPB reports that younger Americans are far more likely to embrace social media, podcasts and generative AI to meet their financial information needs, and that 32% of Americans turn to a financial advisor (such as a CFP professional).
items.quote: Younger Americans are far more likely to embrace social media, podcasts and generative AI to meet their financial information needs.

items.text: A Wealthtender survey reports the channels consumers (all ages, not broken out by age) plan to use to find a financial advisor, including referrals from friends or family (62%), search engines (49.8%), financial institution (49%), referrals from professionals (49.2%), online advisor directories (31.8%), AI search tools (25.4%), and social media (22.2%).
items.quote: Referrals from friends or family 62.00%

items.text: The CFPB reports that Millennials and Gen Z (aged 25-45) are more trusting than older Americans (aged 46-64) of financial information obtained from generative AI tools (44% vs. 26%) and social media (44% vs. 24%).
items.quote: Those aged 25-45 are more trusting than older Americans aged 4664 of the financial information obtained from generative AI tools (44% vs. 26%) and social media (44% vs. 24%).

a2.all.differs_because: No passage states the specific channels and sources that clients under 40 use to find and research a financial advisor. The Schwab and CFPB passages describe channels younger clients use to learn about finances or meet financial information needs (a different purpose than finding/researching an advisor), while the Wealthtender passage describes channels used to find an advisor but for all consumers, not clients under 40.
a2.all.reason: The passages provide related but not exactly matching evidence: younger clients' channels for financial information (Schwab, CFPB) and all-consumer channels for finding an advisor (Wealthtender), so I labeled the cell different_quantity.

a3.all.label: fact

items.text: For the next generation choosing a wealth manager, experience and expertise sit at the top of the wish list, cited by 79% of respondents.
items.quote: When choosing a wealth manager, experience and expertise sit at the top of the next generation's wish list (79%).

items.text: Millennials' financial lives have been shaped by heightened student debt, pandemic-era joblessness, and higher mortgage rates that put home ownership further out of reach, leading some to delay traditional milestones such as getting married, buying a home, and having children.
items.quote: They also have contended with heightened student debt and the economic upheaval of the pandemic... recent higher mortgage rates have put the goal of home ownership further out of reach for some. As a result, some Millennials have delayed traditional milestones such as getting married, buying a home, and having children.

items.text: Competing financial priorities (such as credit card debt, student loans, and caring for family members) materially constrain retirement saving for more than 50% of Gen X, over 75% of Millennials, and above 70% of Gen Z, versus approximately 30% of Baby Boomers.
items.quote: approximately 30% of working Baby Boomers report that competing priorities materially constrain retirement saving; this share rises to more than 50% for Gen X, exceeds 75% for Millennials, and remains above 70% for Gen Z.
items.scope: generations (Gen Z, Millennials, Gen X, Baby Boomers)

items.text: A distinct generational divide persists in how competing financial priorities (credit card debt, paying down student loans, saving for college, caring for family, time out of the workforce, financial hardship, too many monthly expenses) affect retirement savings, with Millennials the most impacted.
items.quote: a distinct generational divide persists in how these competing priorities affect retirement savings... Millennials, for instance, are noted as being the most impacted.

items.text: Across all respondents (not age-specific), the top financial goals or needs for which people would seek a financial advisor's help are retirement planning and income strategies (63%), investment management and portfolio growth (53%), tax planning and optimization (29%), and estate planning and wealth transfer (26%).
items.quote: What are your top 2-3 most important financial goals or needs that you would seek a financial advisor's help with? ... Retirement planning and income strategies 63 ... Investment management and portfolio growth 53 ... Tax planning and optimization 29 ... Estate planning and wealth transfer 26

items.text: Cerulli finds that younger investors are more comfortable directing their own investing through online brokerages, so financial advisors seeking to connect with these prospective clients must articulate benefits outside the investing realm, such as financial planning, lending, and tax services.
items.quote: Younger investors typically are more comfortable directing their own investing through online brokerages (e.g., E*TRADE, Fidelity), meaning financial advisors looking to connect with these prospective clients must be able to articulate benefits outside of the investing realm, such as financial planning, lending, and tax services.

items.text: Schwab's President and CEO states that younger new-to-firm households come in wanting to consolidate loans into a Pledged Asset Line to pay off student debt and to talk about buying a house in the future, reflecting life-stage financial needs.
items.quote: They'll come in and want to consolidate loans into a Pledged Asset Line balance so they can pay off their student debt. They'll talk to us about how to buy a house in the future.

items.text: Schwab states that one-third of retail households who created a financial plan within the last two years are under the age of 40.
items.quote: one-third of retail households who created a financial plan within the last two years are under the age of 40
items.unit: retail households who created a financial plan

items.text: Goldman Sachs Asset Management research finds that major life events - having a child, buying a home, funding college, or managing significant financial hardship - are especially common among younger cohorts and often overlap.
items.quote: Major life events-such as having a child, buying a home, funding college, or managing a significant financial hardship-can materially affect retirement saving. These events are especially common among younger cohorts and often overlap.

items.text: Goldman Sachs Asset Management research shows the financial challenges affecting younger generations' (Gen Z and Millennials) ability to save include credit card debt, paying down student loans, saving for college, caring for and financially supporting family members, and time out of the workforce.
items.quote: Credit card debt Paying down existing loans (student loans, etc) Saving for college (you or others) Caring for and financially supporting family members Time out of the workforce

items.text: BofA Private Bank research finds younger investors (Gen Z and Millennials, ages 21 to 45) allocate more to alternative investments and crypto than older investors and believe traditional stocks and bonds can no longer deliver above-average returns.
items.quote: Younger investors allocate nearly half as much to stocks as older generations, while allocating more to alternatives (fifteen percent 15%) and crypto (thirteen percent 13%) than older investors.

a3.all.reason: The UBS next-generation study directly states the priorities and needs that shape how younger clients choose a wealth manager, and supporting research describes younger generations' competing financial priorities and life-stage needs.

items.text: Schwab states that younger investors' top online resource is YouTube.

a4.all.differs_because: Passages describe the role of digital tools/technology in advisor search and selection for consumers generally (and 'younger investors' at Schwab), not specifically for clients under 40.
a4.all.reason: No passage states how clients under 40 specifically use digital tools to select an advisor; the related evidence concerns advisor-search technology for a broader, non-age-specific population.

a5.all.label: fact

items.text: Nearly half of survey participants (48%) said pricing and overall anticipated costs are among the top three factors that lead them to choose one advisor over others.
items.quote: Nearly half of survey participants (48%) said pricing and overall anticipated costs are among the top three factors that lead them to choose one advisor over others.

items.text: 73% of people consider fee transparency the most important trust factor when choosing an advisor.
items.quote: Our study shows 73% of people consider fee transparency the most important trust factor.

items.text: Cerulli reports that Millennials have better access to low-cost investing options (online brokerages, zero trading fees, index and target-date funds) than any other generation, and that younger investors are typically more comfortable directing their own investing through online brokerages, meaning financial advisors must articulate benefits outside of the investing realm (such as financial planning, lending, and tax services) to attract these prospective clients.
items.quote: Millennials have better access to individual retirement savings plans... and low-cost investing options (e.g., online brokerages, zero trading fees, index and target-date funds) than any other generation... Younger investors typically are more comfortable directing their own investing through online brokerages (e.g., E*TRADE, Fidelity), meaning financial advisors looking to connect with these prospective clients must be able to articulate benefits outside of the investing realm, such as financial planning, lending, and tax services.

a5.all.reason: The Cerulli passage directly addresses younger investors (Millennials, approximating clients under 40) and their gravitation toward low-cost, zero-fee investing options, which is partial evidence of cost sensitivity; however, no passage directly quantifies under-40 clients' sensitivity to fees when specifically choosing an advisor.

a6.all.label: different_quantity

items.quote: The next generation want advisors with not just technical know-how, but the ability to build a rapport with the family and communicate clearly with every generation.

items.text: A Wealthtender survey found that 63% of people consider professional credentials a key factor in determining an advisor's trustworthiness.
items.quote: Our study shows 63% of people consider professional credentials a key factor in determining trustworthiness. Credentials like CFP (Certified Financial Planner) or CFA (Chartered Financial Analyst) require extensive education, rigorous testing, and ongoing professional development.

items.text: The study advises advisor-seekers to prioritize fee transparency, professional credentials, and positive client reviews, and to trust their instincts about communication style and personal comfort level.

a6.all.reason: No passage states the factors for clients under 40 specifically; they are stated for a broader (all survey participants) or different ('next generation') population, so the quantity named is not directly stated.

claims.text: Schwab (2025Q3, period ended September 30, 2025) states that younger clients learn about finances primarily through social media and family, and that being met in those channels is a reason they turn to the firm.

Schwab (2025Q3) states that younger traders turn to it because they recognize trading's potential to help build wealth over time and because of its platforms, tools, education, coaching, expertise, and service.
Bank of America Private Bank's study (published 2026-06-17) finds that 65% of young investors still prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor.

Schwab's CEO (2025Q3) stated that young new-to-firm clients (a third are Gen Zers under age 28) seek financial planning conversations, want to consolidate loans (e.g., into a Pledged Asset Line to pay off student debt), want advice on buying a house in the future, and want to be long-term investors who need help navigating.
For the next generation choosing a wealth manager, experience and expertise sit at the top of the wish list, cited by 79% of next-generation (wealth transfer heirs) respondents.

Cerulli (published 2025-10-29) reports that Millennials' financial lives have been shaped by heightened student debt, pandemic-era joblessness, and higher mortgage rates that put home ownership further out of reach, leading some to delay traditional milestones such as getting married, buying a home, and having children.

Goldman Sachs Asset Management research (published 2025-10-01) finds that competing financial priorities (such as credit card debt, student loans, and caring for family members) materially constrain retirement saving for more than 50% of Gen X, over 75% of Millennials, and above 70% of Gen Z, versus approximately 30% of Baby Boomers.

Goldman Sachs Asset Management research (published 2025-10-01) finds that a distinct generational divide persists in how competing financial priorities (credit card debt, paying down student loans, saving for college, caring for family, time out of the workforce, financial hardship, too many monthly expenses) affect retirement savings, with Millennials noted as the most impacted generation.

A Wealthtender survey (published 2025-08-13) reports that across all respondents (not age-specific), the top financial goals or needs for which people would seek a financial advisor's help are retirement planning and income strategies (63%), investment management and portfolio growth (53%), tax planning and optimization (29%), and estate planning and wealth transfer (26%).

Schwab's President and CEO (2025Q3) states that younger new-to-firm households come in wanting to consolidate loans into a Pledged Asset Line to pay off student debt and to talk about buying a house in the future, reflecting life-stage financial needs.
Schwab (2025Q3) states that one-third of retail households who created a financial plan within the last two years are under the age of 40.

Goldman Sachs Asset Management research (published 2025-10-01) finds that major life events - having a child, buying a home, funding college, or managing significant financial hardship - are especially common among younger cohorts and often overlap.

Goldman Sachs Asset Management research (published 2025-10-01) shows the financial challenges affecting younger generations' (Gen Z and Millennials) ability to save include credit card debt, paying down student loans, saving for college, caring for and financially supporting family members, and time out of the workforce.

BofA Private Bank research (published 2026-06-17) finds younger investors (Gen Z and Millennials, ages 21 to 45) allocate more to alternative investments and crypto than older investors and believe traditional stocks and bonds can no longer deliver above-average returns.

A Wealthtender survey (published 2025-08-13) found that nearly half of survey participants (48%) said pricing and overall anticipated costs are among the top three factors that lead them to choose one advisor over others.
A Wealthtender study (published 2025-08-13) reports that 73% of people consider fee transparency the most important trust factor when choosing an advisor.

Cerulli (published 2025-10-29) reports that Millennials have better access to low-cost investing options (online brokerages, zero trading fees, index and target-date funds) than any other generation, and that younger investors are typically more comfortable directing their own investing through online brokerages, meaning financial advisors must articulate benefits outside of the investing realm (such as financial planning, lending, and tax services) to attract these prospective clients.
According to the 2026 Bank of America Private Bank Study of Wealthy Americans (published 2026-06-17), 47% of young investors use AI to research companies or markets.

Cerulli Associates research (published 2025-10-29) finds that while older investors tend to be more advisor-reliant, younger investors prefer to retain a greater degree of control of at least part of their investing lives.
A CFPB survey (period 2025) found those aged 25-45 are more trusting than older Americans aged 46-64 of financial information obtained from generative AI tools (44% vs. 26%).

Fidelity's 2025 Investor Insights Study (published 2025-10-09) states wealthy next-generation (Gen X, Y, Z) households seek transparency in advisor compensation and broader life guidance beyond investment management, plus emerging investment products, when working with advisors.
Bank of America (period 2025) reports 70% of next-gen clients seek to transfer investment assets and investment relationships to a bank in the next year.

Schwab's CEO Rick Wurster (2025Q3) states younger clients learn about finances primarily through social media and family, and Schwab meets them in the channels where they turn for information about investing.

The 2026 Bank of America Private Bank Study finds that 65% of young investors (Gen Z and Millennials) still prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor, even as 47% use AI to research companies or markets and 87% are comfortable with advisors using AI to help manage portfolios. Why it might matter: the source states 47% of young investors use AI to research companies or markets, illustrating why their continued human-advisor preference is notable.

Bank of America Private Bank's 2026 Study of Wealthy Americans (period 2026) reports that 65% of younger investors (Gen Z and Millennials) still prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor. Why it might matter: the context notes that 47% of young investors use AI to research companies or markets and 87% are comfortable with advisors using AI to help manage portfolios, highlighting the contrast with their continued human-advisor preference.

Cerulli (published 2026-03-25) finds that the mass-affluent segment ($100,000 to $2 million in financial assets), which is typically younger and less advised, seeks involved advisor relationships. Why it might matter: the source states this $25 trillion market, comprising 46.9 million households, will benefit providers that can best offer streamlined advisory services at scale.

Cerulli (period 2025) finds that younger investors are typically more comfortable directing their own investing through online brokerages, meaning financial advisors looking to connect with these prospective clients must be able to articulate benefits outside of the investing realm, such as financial planning, lending, and tax services. Why it might matter: the source notes that Millennial children of wealthy clients represent a clear long-term opportunity for advisors seeking to connect with prospective clients.

Schwab (2025Q3) states that younger clients (Gen Z investors) learn about finances primarily through social media and family, which is one reason they turn to Schwab. Why it might matter: Schwab's CEO explains that one reason these young clients turn to Schwab is because Schwab meets them in the channels where they turn for information about investing.

Schwab (2025Q3) states that younger investors' top online resource is YouTube, and Schwab is the number one financial services firm on YouTube by followers. Why it might matter: the context notes that younger investors at Schwab are highly engaged in building their wealth over the long term, and that the average age of Schwab's clients continues to get younger.

Fidelity's 2025 Investor Insights Study reports that wealthy next generation households (generation X, Y, and Z) are reshaping the advisor-client relationship and, while they value advisors, seek transparency in advisor compensation, broader life guidance beyond investment management, and emerging investment products. Why it might matter: the source states the advisor-client relationship is being reshaped with a focus on holistic financial planning, life goal achievement, and non-traditional investment strategies, and that advisors must adapt to serve this generation's distinctive demands.

The CFPB (period 2025) reports that Millennials and Gen Z are more likely than older adults to act on financial information they encounter without further validation, especially from online sources; those aged 25-45 are more trusting than older Americans (aged 46-64) of financial information from generative AI tools (44% vs. 26%) and social media (44% vs. 24%). Why it might matter: the source notes that survey respondents are less comfortable acting on financial information from news outlets (47%), generative AI tools (38%), and social media (37%).

items.text: Morgan Stanley's strategic-update deck lists "Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning" and "Founders Wealth Strategies" among the capabilities the integrated firm provides to clients across their growth cycles, under the "Preserve Wealth" and "Invest for the Future" stages.
items.quote: Invest for the Future / Financial Wellness and Employee Benefits / Founders Wealth Strategies / Preserve Wealth / Full-Service Wealth Advice and Asset Allocation / Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning

items.text: CEO Ted Pick stated the firm is using its scale to invest in broadening capabilities for financial advisors, including family office and OCIO, as part of retaining and serving wealthy clients.
items.quote: We are using our scale to invest in broadening capabilities for FAs that are difficult for others to replicate: alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, digitized assets, family office and OCIO, and tailored lending.

a3.MS.reason: Passages describe the firm's family office, trust & estate planning, and founders wealth strategy capabilities, which are how it retains relationships as wealth passes to next generations.

a5.MS.label: fact

items.text: Morgan Stanley's strategic presentation lays out capabilities to serve clients throughout their growth cycle, including 'Founders Wealth Strategies', 'Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning', and 'Financial Wellness and Employee Benefits' for founders and employees.
items.quote: Founders / Employees ... Financial Wellness and Employee Benefits ... Founders Wealth Strategies ... Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning

items.text: Morgan Stanley's strategic presentation includes capabilities to help founders and early-stage/private companies unlock liquidity, including 'Private Shares Trading & Lending' and 'IPO Execution and Support Services'.
items.quote: Unlock Liquidity / Private Shares Trading & Lending / IPO Execution and Support Services / Optimize for Growth

items.text: Morgan Stanley's expanded partnership with Carta offers its advice-based services to founders and family offices throughout a company's journey from private to public state.
items.quote: What Carta now does is it's been interested in being able to offer these services not just to the individual founders ... but throughout their entire journey. We're offering our advice-based service to those individuals ... We've done a lot of work on trying to service founders, on trying to service family offices.

items.text: Morgan Stanley deepened its competitive moats through an expanded collaboration with Carta in private markets and through announced partnerships with Zero Hash in digital assets.
items.quote: we continue to invest, deepening our competitive moats in areas like our expanded collaboration with Carta in private markets and in digital assets through announced partnerships with Zero Hash.

items.text: Morgan Stanley's strategic initiatives include the acquisition of EquityZen, an expanded partnership with Carta, and a collaboration with Zero Hash, which the firm frames as innovation to widen its competitive moats.
items.quote: Strategic initiatives such as our recent acquisition of EquityZen, expanded partnership with Carta, and collaboration with Zero Hash all reflect our commitment to innovation.

items.text: Morgan Stanley is investing in broadening capabilities for financial advisors, including alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, digitized assets, family office and OCIO, and tailored lending.
items.quote: We are using our scale to invest in broadening capabilities for FAs that are difficult for others to replicate: alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, digitized assets, family office and OCIO, and tailored lending.

items.text: Morgan Stanley is working on products to fill gaps and provide a more democratized offering of alternatives across the platform, including to its retail client base.
items.quote: we are looking also at places to help fill these gaps and to help you provide a more democratized offering ... there's great opportunity there for us and more broadly just for those alternatives across the platform to go to our retail client base.

items.text: Morgan Stanley is offering new products to clients such as evergreen products and products that allow for lower denomination size as it works to grow alternatives across the platform.
items.quote: We're offering new products to our clients, such as evergreen products and products that allow for lower denomination size.

items.text: Morgan Stanley invests in E*TRADE and the self-directed channel, and in its workplace product, as part of its client acquisition funnel.
items.quote: We're investing in E*TRADE. The self-directed channel is very busy ... the workplace product where we added another $20 billion.

items.text: Morgan Stanley describes offering financial advice and financial wellness to clients, matching advisers to clients with technology, and offering more products, alternatives and solutions for individuals at different points in their life cycle.
items.quote: what kind of financial advice and financial wellness can you offer to the clients ... we have a greater ability to match advisers to the right clients ... we're able to offer more products, alternatives, different types of solutions as well as financial advice broadly for different types of individuals at different points in their life cycle.

a5.MS.reason: The passages describe specific products, services and platforms (founders strategies, family office, private shares trading, Carta/Zero Hash/EquityZen partnerships, E*TRADE, alternatives/democratized offerings) used to attract and serve next-generation clients.

a6.MS.label: fact

items.text: Morgan Stanley's integrated firm model is positioned to serve clients through their growth cycles, including 'Founders Wealth Strategies' and, for the 'Preserve Wealth' stage, full-service wealth advice and asset allocation plus 'Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning'.
items.quote: Founders Wealth Strategies / Preserve Wealth / Full-Service Wealth Advice and Asset Allocation / Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning

items.text: Morgan Stanley highlights Family Office, OCIO (outsourced chief investment officer) and Tailored Lending as offerings.
items.quote: Family Office, OCIO, Tailored Lending

items.text: Morgan Stanley offers 'family office infrastructure solutions' for ultra-high net worth clients.
items.quote: for ultra-high net worth family office infrastructure solutions

items.text: Morgan Stanley is investing in broadening capabilities for financial advisors that are difficult for others to replicate, including family office and OCIO, and tailored lending.
items.quote: alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, digitized assets, family office and OCIO, and tailored lending

items.text: Morgan Stanley has done substantial work to service founders and family offices.
items.quote: We've done a lot of work on trying to service founders, on trying to service family offices.

items.text: Morgan Stanley's integrated firm has a business mix that can support clients throughout an entire life cycle, with Morgan Stanley at Work positioning it as an early trusted advisor to private companies and their employees.
items.quote: We have scaled capabilities and a business mix that can support our clients throughout an entire life cycle.

items.text: The integrated firm proposition allows Morgan Stanley to act as a trusted advisor to a founder, whose relationship with a wealth manager can then work with the investment banker across generations of wealth needs.
items.quote: you may be trusted advisor to a founder, and that founder may have a relationship with a wealth manager, and that wealth manager then can work with the investment banker

a6.MS.reason: Multiple passages describe how Morgan Stanley engages families and facilitates multi-generational wealth planning through family office, trust & estate planning, OCIO, and lifecycle services.

a7.MS.label: fact

items.text: Morgan Stanley's strategic deck describes the integrated firm as delivering capabilities throughout clients' growth cycles, listing 'Founders Wealth Strategies,' 'Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning,' 'Preserve Wealth,' 'Full-Service Wealth Advice and Asset Allocation,' and 'Financial Wellness and Employee Benefits' as offerings for founders/employees to invest for the future and preserve wealth.
items.quote: Corporates / Founders / Employees / Early Stage / Public Company / Invest for the Future / Financial Wellness and Employee Benefits / Founders Wealth Strategies / Preserve Wealth / Full-Service Wealth Advice and Asset Allocation / Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning / Unlock Liquidity / Private Shares Trading & Lending / IPO Execution and Support Services / Optimize for Growth

items.text: CEO Ted Pick stated the firm is focused on both public and private ecosystems, augmented by the EquityZen acquisition, with the objective of covering growth companies and their employees from founding to public maturity while broadening access to private companies.
items.quote: We are focused on both the public and the private ecosystems, augmented by our recent acquisition of EquityZen. The objective is to cover growth companies and their employees from founding to their public maturity while broadening access for investors to the growing stack of private companies.

items.text: CFO Sharon Yeshaya explained that IPO-related flows have a tail, noting the firm understands the full cap table (including early investors and endowments) and can convert stock received at IPO through a transfer agent into a Morgan Stanley advice-based relationship, capturing wealth across the cap table.
items.quote: we have a full cap table. We understand early investors. And you can think, for example, of an endowment that might receive a stock associated with an IPO. He or she might take that and put it through from a transfer agent into a Morgan Stanley advice-based relationship.

items.text: CFO Sharon Yeshaya described the exclusive partnership with Carta, whereby Carta refers private companies and their stock plans to Morgan Stanley as they go public, creating a seamless experience and opportunities to build out relationships through that transition.
items.quote: we have an exclusive partnership with Carta, which means that they will refer those private different stock plans or different corporate companies to Morgan Stanley as they move into going public... we are committed to doing as we go through that transition is to make sure that it's a seamless experience for those clients.

items.text: CEO Ted Pick described Solium as a 'hidden gem' type acquisition that can be brought in to help transform where the firm is going with clients, within the core strategy of raise, manage, and allocate capital.
items.quote: some of them may be more hidden gems like a Solium, which I thought was ingenious, that can be brought in to actually help transform where the firm is going to go with clients.

items.text: CEO Ted Pick stated that investments in self-directed and Workplace channels drive the firm's differentiated client acquisition funnel, reaching over 19 million relationships and adding over $250 billion of net new assets annually, on track toward $10 trillion plus of total client assets.
items.quote: In Wealth Management, investments in our self-directed and Workplace channels drive our differentiated client acquisition funnel. Today, with our expanded offering, we reach over 19 million relationships and have added net new assets of over $250 billion in each of the past two years on track to delivering $10 trillion plus of total client assets.

a7.MS.reason: Multiple passages contain leadership statements and strategic initiatives (family office/trust & estate planning, founders wealth strategies, EquityZen, Carta, workplace funnel) indicating commitment to capturing wealth across client growth and wealth-transfer cycles.

a8.MS.label: fact

items.text: Morgan Stanley defines Wealth Management net new assets as client asset inflows, inclusive of interest, dividends and asset acquisitions, less client asset outflows, excluding the impact of business combinations/divestitures and fees and commissions.
items.quote: Wealth Management net new assets represent client asset inflows, inclusive of interest, dividends and asset acquisitions, less client asset outflows, and exclude the impact of business combinations/divestitures and the impact of fees and commissions.
items.definition: client asset inflows, inclusive of interest, dividends and asset acquisitions, less client asset outflows, and exclude the impact of business combinations/divestitures and the impact of fees and commissions

items.text: Morgan Stanley's total client assets across Wealth and Investment Management grew to $9.3 trillion at year-end 2025, supported by over $350 billion in net new assets.
items.quote: Total client assets in Wealth and Investment Management grew to $9.3 trillion, supported by over $350 billion in net new assets.
items.unit: trillion USD (total client assets, Wealth and Investment Management)

items.text: Morgan Stanley's total client assets across Wealth and Investment Management stood at $10 trillion in the second quarter of 2026, fulfilling a strategic milestone.
items.quote: Across Wealth and Investment Management, total client assets stand at $10 trillion, fulfilling a Morgan Stanley strategic milestone.
items.unit: trillion USD (total client assets, Wealth and Investment Management)

items.text: Morgan Stanley's Wealth Management total client assets stood at $8 trillion in the second quarter of 2026.
items.quote: The business generated a record of $8.9 billion in revenues and total client assets stand at $8 trillion.

items.text: Morgan Stanley reported $8.4 trillion in client assets in the third quarter of 2026.
items.quote: Today, we have $8.4 trillion in client assets and serve nearly 21 million relationships.

items.text: Morgan Stanley reported full-year 2025 net new assets of $356.3 billion, versus $251.7 billion in 2024.
Morgan Stanley reported full-year 2024 net new assets of $251.7 billion.
Morgan Stanley reported fourth quarter 2025 net new assets of $122.3 billion.
Morgan Stanley reported first quarter 2026 net new assets of $118 billion and fee-based flows of $54 billion.
items.quote: driving industry-leading growth with $118 billion of net new assets and $54 billion of fee-based flows.

items.text: Morgan Stanley reported record second quarter 2026 net new assets of $148 billion.
items.quote: net new assets were a record of $148 billion.

items.text: Morgan Stanley reported third quarter 2026 net new assets of $232 billion.
items.quote: net new assets of $232 billion reflect the strength of our core business and the differentiated growth opportunities created by Workplace and the integrated firm.

items.text: Morgan Stanley stated it retains 99% of its clients, and that 60% of advisor-led assets are associated with clients having an average relationship duration of 20 years.
items.quote: 60% of advisor-led assets are associated with clients who have an average duration of 20 years. We retain 99% of our clients, reflecting their enduring trust in Morgan Stanley.

items.text: Morgan Stanley noted greater asset retention from its Workplace channel in the first quarter of 2026, as vested assets were retained and migrated into the advisor-led channel.
items.quote: what we saw in Workplace this quarter is greater retention of the assets that vested... we saw greater asset retention from Workplace, which translated into NNA.

a8.MS.reason: The passages disclose net new assets (the proxy metric), total and Wealth Management client assets, and a client retention rate, all of which serve as proxies for wealth-transfer capture.

a9.MS.label: fact

items.text: Morgan Stanley's strategic update deck presents 'Founders Wealth Strategies,' 'Preserve Wealth,' 'Full-Service Wealth Advice and Asset Allocation,' and 'Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning' among the capabilities it offers to founders/employees across their growth cycle, alongside 'Unlock Liquidity' (private shares trading and lending) and IPO execution services.
items.quote:
Founders Wealth Strategies

Preserve Wealth

items.text: Morgan Stanley states that 60% of its advisor-led assets are associated with clients who have an average relationship duration of 20 years, and that it retains 99% of its clients, reflecting enduring trust.
items.quote: 60% of advisor-led assets are associated with clients who have an average duration of 20 years. We retain 99% of our clients, reflecting their enduring trust in Morgan Stanley.

a9.MS.reason: The passages contain Morgan Stanley's own statements about its wealth preservation, family office, trust & estate planning capabilities and long-tenured client relationships, which bear directly on its preparedness for generational wealth transfer.

Industry research: UBS estimates USD 83 trillion in private wealth will change hands globally over the next two to three decades, the largest transfer of wealth in modern history.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: In the third quarter of 2025, Schwab stated that client assets are more concentrated among older generations today, while the average age of its clients continues to get younger.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: For the third quarter of 2026, Schwab reported that roughly 75% of assets are retained in a wealth transfer event, and that roughly 80% of retail assets are held by ultra-high net worth and high net worth households.
The Charles Schwab Corporation: In the third quarter of 2026, Schwab stated its retention rate around wealth transfers is extremely high, and that it is winning assets with all generations.
The Charles Schwab Corporation: In the fourth quarter of 2025, Schwab stated the average age of its client has fallen by about 10 years in the last decade and is now in the 40s.
The Charles Schwab Corporation: In the third quarter of 2025, Schwab cited industry research showing Gen Z is 45% more likely to start investing by age 21 as compared to Millennials.
The Charles Schwab Corporation: For the third quarter of 2026, Schwab reported that approximately 70% of new-to-firm retail households are Gen Z and Millennials.
The Charles Schwab Corporation: In the fourth quarter of 2024, Schwab stated that 33% of new-to-firm retail households are under age 30 and more than 50% are under age 40.
The Charles Schwab Corporation: Gen Z investors comprise nearly a third of new retail client accounts opened in 2025, and nearly 60% are under age 40.
The Charles Schwab Corporation: Schwab's investor day materials report that 61% of new clients are Gen Z and Millennial investors.

Edward Jones: In its second quarter 2025 10-Q, Edward Jones stated that an aging client base is one of the demographic factors influencing elevated asset outflows and the downward trend in net new assets.
Edward Jones: In its fiscal 2025 10-K, Edward Jones stated that the evolving financial services industry and generational wealth transfer include changing client demographics, preferences and values.

Edward Jones: In its fiscal 2025 10-K, Edward Jones stated that generational wealth transfer is characterized in part by changing client expectations for expanded product offerings and technology needs.
Industry research: Cerulli projects Generation Xers will inherit $39 trillion and Millennials will inherit $46 trillion.

Industry research: Cerulli projects women in the Baby Boomer and older generations will receive $40 trillion in 'horizontal' transfers as they outlive their husbands, and women in younger generations will receive $47 trillion of the wealth transferred intergenerationally.
Industry research: Cerulli notes wealth is now more likely to be held by older households.

Industry research: Cerulli notes notable differences in service preferences among women and next-generation clients compared to current client demographics, likely to shift marketshare to firms best prepared to meet recipients' needs.
Industry research: UBS attributes the wealth transfer to aging demographics, longer life expectancies, and decades of rising asset prices.

Morgan Stanley: Its strategic-update deck lists Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning and Founders Wealth Strategies among the capabilities the integrated firm provides to clients across their growth cycles, under the Preserve Wealth and Invest for the Future stages.

Morgan Stanley: In the fourth quarter of 2025, CEO Ted Pick stated the firm is using its scale to invest in broadening capabilities for financial advisors that are difficult for others to replicate, including family office and OCIO, and tailored lending, as part of retaining and serving wealthy clients.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: In the third quarter of 2026, Schwab stated its retail business is built to win across generations and that its retention rate around wealth transfers is extremely high, positioning the firm to continue serving future generations when wealth is passed on.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: In the third quarter of 2026, Schwab stated that roughly 80% of retail assets are held by ultra-high net worth and high net worth households, which positions it to serve future generations when that wealth is passed on.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: In the second quarter of 2025, Schwab stated it is enhancing its tax, trust, and estate capabilities, including plans to offer Wealth.com's estate planning tools to retail clients, to help retain relationships as wealth transfers to heirs.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: In the first quarter of 2025, Schwab announced a strategic investment in Wealth.com, a leader in digital estate planning, to enhance estate planning capabilities and experience for clients.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: In the fourth quarter of 2025, Schwab stated it took an ownership stake in Wealth.com and began rolling out its estate analysis capability to specialists, giving more tools to help clients integrate estate planning into their investment life.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: In the first quarter of 2026, Schwab stated it increased its strategic investment in Wealth.com, which it is using to bring AI-powered estate planning tools to clients, and is working to launch AI-powered tax planning capability.

Edward Jones: In its fiscal 2025 10-K, the Partnership stated that its new-client initiatives include a new digital platform focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors, alongside High Net Worth and Workplace initiatives.

Edward Jones: In its fiscal 2025 10-K, the Partnership stated it seeks to address its strategic risks, most notably competition for clients and personnel in light of the evolving financial services industry and generational wealth transfer, through its initiatives to deliver enhanced value and impact for current and potential clients, colleagues and communities.

Edward Jones: In its fiscal 2025 10-K, the Partnership stated that Business Resource Group members and other colleagues come together to discover ways to serve clients and future clients more deeply, especially as demographics and needs change.

Raymond James Financial: Its Private Wealth Advisor designation program, launched in September 2022, provides training, coaching, and a peer network for advisors who specialize in high-net-worth clients (generally those with at least $5 million in investable assets); as of September 2026 nearly 450 advisors had earned the designation.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: Per its fiscal 2025 10-K, Schwab's financial consultant career achievement plan is a noncontributory, unfunded, nonqualified retirement plan under which an eligible financial consultant receives earned cash payments after retirement, contingent upon meeting performance levels, tenure, age, and client transitioning requirements; full vesting occurs when a financial consultant reaches age 60 with at least ten years of service.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: Per its fiscal 2025 10-K, Schwab's Advisor Services segment offers advisors help to establish their own independent practices, providing access to business start-up and transition consultants, technology engineers, and dedicated service teams throughout their transition.
The Charles Schwab Corporation: Schwab noted it has some 3,000 financial advisors in-house, many of whom hold CFPs.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: Schwab plans to hire thousands more financial consultants to serve retail investors across its 400 branches, with plans to open more than 20 million client accounts in the next five years.

Which firm appears most prepared: The comparison can be made only partially on this evidence. The firms disclose very different evidence for preparedness, and no common metric for wealth-transfer capture is published across all five, so no single firm can be ranked as most prepared on a like-for-like basis. On the specific grounds that are disclosed, Schwab is the only firm that publishes a direct retention metric for wealth transfers (approximately 75% of assets retained in a wealth transfer event), and it states its retail business is built to win across generations with an extremely high retention rate; Morgan Stanley discloses a 99% client retention rate and 20-year relationship durations but does not quantify wealth-transfer retention specifically; Merrill discloses leadership in next-generation advisor talent (446 advisors on the 2025 Forbes list) but not a wealth-transfer retention figure; Raymond James discloses intergenerational wealth strategies and advisor succession retention but no wealth-transfer retention percentage; and Edward Jones discloses that generational wealth transfers outside the firm are a drag on net new assets, the opposite evidence of the other firms. Because these measures are not defined on a common basis (different units, scopes, and periods), they cannot be validly compared or ranked across firms.

items.text: Morgan Stanley's Total Client Assets, defined as the sum of Wealth Management client assets and Investment Management AUM, reached $10.5 trillion as of the third quarter of 2026, per CFO Sharon Yeshaya.
items.quote: With $10.5 trillion in total client assets across Wealth and Investment Management, we have the foundation to build on as we close out the year.
items.definition: Total Client Assets represent the sum of the reported Wealth Management ('WM') client assets and Investment Management ('IM') assets under management ('AuM').

claims.text: The comparison: The client assets per advisor figures across the five firms cannot be validly compared side by side, because the underlying client-asset measures and advisor-count measures differ by firm. Morgan Stanley's advisor count is labeled 'Wealth Management representatives' (15,950 at December 31, 2020, MS-SUPP-2020Q4#1), and its asset measure is Total Client Assets, the sum of Wealth Management client assets and Investment Management AUM (MS-DECK-2026-strategic-update#28). Schwab reports no financial-advisor headcount; it reports full-time-equivalent employees (approximately 33,000, SCHW-10K-2025#49) and, for Advisor Services, more than 16,000 independent advisory firms (SCHW-TR-2026Q3#10), with client assets that include custodial assets of independent RIAs (SCHW-10K-2025#26). Edward Jones counts 'financial advisors (actual)' (EDJ-10Q-2026Q1#51), many of whom are employees (EDJ-10K-2025#59), and measures 'assets under care' ($2.6 trillion in 2Q26, EDJ-10Q-2026Q2#61). Merrill's advisor count is 'Total wealth advisors' including advisors across all wealth management businesses in GWIM and Consumer Banking (18,916 at 2023Q4, BAC-SUPP-2023Q4#2), which is broader than Merrill alone, and its AUM is defined as managed assets under advisory and/or discretion of GWIM (BAC-SUPP-2026Q3#54). Raymond James excludes RCS-division advisors from its financial advisor metric even though their client assets are included in AUA (RJF-10K-2025#228), and reports Private Client Group AUA of $1.67 trillion with 8,943 advisors as of September 30, 2025 (RJF-10K-2025#9). Because client-asset definitions (total client assets, total client assets under care, AUM, AUA), advisor-count definitions, and covered business scopes differ, and the per-advisor figures are not based on a common definition, the figures are not comparable.

a1.MS.label: fact

items.text: Morgan Stanley disclosed that for certain revenue-producing employees in the Wealth Management and Investment Management business segments, compensation is largely paid on the basis of formulaic payouts that link employee compensation to revenues.
items.quote: For certain revenue-producing employees in the Wealth Management and Investment Management business segments, compensation is largely paid on the basis of formulaic payouts that link employee compensation to revenues.
items.scope: Wealth Management and Investment Management business segments

items.text: Morgan Stanley disclosed that deferred compensation for financial advisors in the Wealth Management business segment is generally composed of 75% cash-based awards and 25% stock-based awards.
items.quote: Deferred compensation for financial advisors in the Wealth Management business segment is generally composed of 75% cash-based awards and 25% stock-based awards.

items.text: Morgan Stanley disclosed that its compensation and benefits expenses include base salaries and fixed allowances, formulaic programs, discretionary incentive compensation, amortization of deferred cash and equity awards, changes in the fair value of referenced notional DCP investments, carried interest allocated to employees, severance costs, and other items such as health and welfare benefits.
items.quote: Compensation and benefits expenses include base salaries and fixed allowances, formulaic programs, discretionary incentive compensation, amortization of deferred cash and equity awards, changes in the fair value of the referenced notional DCP investments, carried interest allocated to employees, severance costs, and other items such as health and welfare benefits.

items.text: Morgan Stanley disclosed that employees (including financial advisors) are permitted to allocate the value of their deferred cash-based awards among a menu of notional investments, selected by the firm, that includes fixed income, equity, commodity and money market funds.
items.quote: Employees are permitted to allocate the value of their deferred cash-based awards among a menu of notional investments, whereby the value of their awards will track the performance of the referenced notional investments. The menu of investments, which is selected by the Firm, includes fixed income, equity, commodity and money market funds.
items.scope: Wealth Management financial advisors (and other employees)
items.definition: DCP - Employee deferred cash-based compensation plans linked to investment performance

items.text: Morgan Stanley disclosed that an advisor serviced through a Morgan Stanley Virtual Advisor (MSVA) is paid a base salary plus a discretionary bonus and does not retain any portion of the Morgan Stanley Advisory Fee.
items.quote: If your account is serviced through a Morgan Stanley Virtual Advisor ("MSVA"), your MSVA is paid a base salary plus a discretionary bonus and does not retain any portion of the Morgan Stanley Advisory Fee.

items.text: Morgan Stanley disclosed that the amount of the advisory fee a client pays is a factor used in calculating the compensation paid to the client's Financial Advisor, and that Financial Advisors have a financial incentive not to reduce fees.
items.quote: The amount of the fee you pay is a factor we use in calculating the compensation we pay your Financial Advisor. Therefore, Financial Advisors have a financial incentive not to reduce fees.

items.text: A Morgan Stanley executive disclosed that the firm will increase the cash component of its advisor compensation.
items.quote: As previously announced, we will also increase the cash component of our advisor compensation.

items.text: InvestmentNews reported that Morgan Stanley is increasing a pay threshold for advisors by 10% in 2027, meaning advisors have to generate that much more revenue to see the same pay next year.
items.quote: As it has in the past, Morgan Stanley is increasing a pay threshold for advisors by 10% in 2027, meaning advisors have to generate that much more revenue to see the same pay next year.

items.text: InvestmentNews reported that Morgan Stanley has taken a small amount of an advisor's gross revenue, called it deferred compensation, and required advisors to stay for years in order to vest.
items.quote: Giants like Morgan Stanley for years have taken a small amount of an advisor's gross revenue, called it deferred compensation, and required advisors to stay for years in order to vest.

a1.MS.reason: Multiple passages describe how Morgan Stanley structures advisor compensation (formulaic payouts, deferred compensation mix, DCP mechanics, MSVA pay, fee-based incentives, and 2027 threshold changes), so these are facts.

claims.text: Merrill: Its 2026 ADV discloses that an Advisor earns compensation based on revenue Merrill earns from the Merrill Lynch Fee, other fees and costs, Sales Charges on brokerage account transactions, and referrals to Affiliates. | Advisors are eligible for a compensation award, payable over a defined period, from an incentive program based on meeting prior-year growth targets in new households and in assets and liabilities; an Advisor is subject to a reduction in their incentive compensation grid if they fail to achieve growth in the assets and liabilities component for two consecutive years. | Advisors do not receive additional compensation from advisory client assets held in the Cash Sweep Program. | Advisors joining from other firms generally receive payments (salary guarantees, upfront awards, deferred payments, recruitment loans) based largely on the size of their prior-firm business, conditioned on assets in accounts they service at Merrill. | Merrill's Advisor Development Program recruiting page discloses base salary and unlimited earning potential. | Elements of field management compensation are based on revenues to Merrill and on advisors meeting strategic goals. | Recommending Style Manager Strategies with no or lower Manager Fees can let an Advisor negotiate a higher Merrill Lynch Fee Rate.
